title: Pao de Queijo
subtitle: Brazilian cheese bread balls made with tapioca flour
excerpt: Light, chewy cheese rolls made from tapioca flour, naturally gluten-free and ready in under 40 minutes. These are eaten for breakfast across Brazil and at every gathering as a snack. The outside crisps up while the inside stays soft and stretchy.
sourceNotes: Pao de queijo originated in the state of Minas Gerais in Brazil during the eighteenth century, when enslaved workers began making bread from cassava starch after wheat imports became scarce. The cheese version became popular across Brazil in the twentieth century and is now eaten for breakfast and as a snack throughout the country.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked balls on a tray, then transfer to a bag. Bake from frozen at 200C for 30 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: The dough scales well. Make a double batch and freeze half for quick breakfasts.

glossaryTerms.definition: A starchy flour made from cassava root. It gives pao de queijo their characteristic chewy, stretchy interior and crisp exterior. Tapioca flour is naturally gluten-free.

content.text: This recipe makes 24 rolls and takes about 35 minutes in total. The dough comes together in minutes and needs no resting time. You can roll the balls by hand and put them straight in the oven, or freeze them raw for baking later.

Heat your oven to 200C (180C fan). Line two baking trays with baking paper.
Place the butter, oil and 150ml whole milk in a small saucepan. Heat over medium heat until the butter has melted and the mixture is just coming to a simmer. Do not boil.
Pour the hot liquid over the tapioca flour in a large bowl, along with 1 tsp salt. Stir well until the flour absorbs the liquid and forms a rough dough. Leave to cool for 5 minutes.
Add the beaten eggs and 150g finely grated strong cheddar or Parmesan to the dough. Mix until completely combined. The dough will be sticky but should hold together.
With lightly dampened hands, roll tablespoon-sized portions of dough into balls. Place on the lined trays with a little space between each.
Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until puffed and golden with a light crust. Eat warm; they are best within 30 minutes of baking, though they reheat well in a hot oven for 5 minutes.

attrs.cause: Oven temperature was too low, or the dough was too cold when it went in
attrs.fix: Make sure the oven is fully preheated to 200C before baking. If the dough sat in the fridge, bring it to room temperature before rolling and baking.

attrs.symptom: Dough is too wet to roll into balls
attrs.cause: Eggs were large, or the milk and butter mixture was not hot enough to cook the flour
attrs.fix: Add an extra tablespoon of tapioca flour at a time and mix until the dough becomes workable. Chilling for 15 minutes also firms it up enough to roll.

attrs.cause: This is actually normal for pao de queijo; the steam creates air pockets in the centre
attrs.fix: Nothing to fix. A slightly hollow centre with a chewy wall is the correct texture. If the centre is completely raw, bake for a further 5 minutes.

content.text: In Brazil, pao de queijo are as everyday as a slice of toast. Padarias (bakeries) sell them warm from the oven all morning. They are eaten at breakfast with a coffee, passed round at parties and taken on long drives as a snack. In Minas Gerais, where they come from, they are made with a sharp local cheese called queijo minas curado. Outside Brazil, Parmesan or mature cheddar are the closest match.
